intro.title: Constructing Low-Inference, Time-Bound Observations
paragraphs: This guide formalizes a fill-in-the-blank process for producing low-inference observational statements: descriptions restricted to verifiable sensory data (what was seen/heard), anchored to concrete time and context, and free of trait labels or motive attributions. The approach synthesizes findings from behavioral observation, psycholinguistics, and affect-regulation research. Linguistic abstraction increases biased social inference (https://www.uni-muenster.de/imperia/md/content/psyifp/aeechterhoff/vorlesungkommunikation/semin_fiedler_cogfunctoflingcategor_jpsp_1989.pdf); concreteness improves comprehension (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6353691/; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8773921/); and affect labeling is associated with reduced limbic reactivity (https://sanlab.psych.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/31/2015/05/Lieberman_AL-2007.pdf).

Perspective-taking and I-language are linked to lower perceived hostility in communication contexts (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5961625/). Research on basic psychological needs provides relevant context for why clear description may matter in interpersonal settings: autonomy/competence (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5050353/; https://selfdeterminationtheory.org/topics/basic-psychological-needs/) and belonging/social connection (https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/surgeon-general-social-connection-advisory.pdf).

items: Recorder criterion: report only what a camera/microphone could capture (verbatim words, visible actions, measurable outcomes). Behavioral observation emphasizes observable units to aid reliability (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4766977/).
Time- and context-bound: specify when/where (e.g., “On Tue 15:10 in the team room…”). Concreteness improves comprehension and reduces ambiguity (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6353691/).
Avoid absolutes (“always/never/constantly”): prefer frequency, duration, or counts (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8773921/).

No mind-reading or motive attributions (e.g., “to hurt me,” “on purpose”): hostile-attribution tendencies relate to aggressive/negative responding (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4243523/; https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.778695/full).

Quantify when feasible: counts, durations, latency, intensity (e.g., decibels). Linguistic abstraction inflates inference; measurables support shared description (https://www.uni-muenster.de/imperia/md/content/psyifp/aeechterhoff/vorlesungkommunikation/semin_fiedler_cogfunctoflingcategor_jpsp_1989.pdf).

content.html: Observations describe events; other components (feelings/needs/requests) are handled elsewhere in the app. Separating description from evaluation aligns with evidence on perspective-taking/I-language (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5961625/).

items: Anchor the scene: “On [DATE] at [TIME] in [PLACE], …” (concreteness advantage: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6353691/).
Describe only what was sensed: “I saw/heard [ACTOR] [ACTION/WORDS].” Behavioral observation favors observable units (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4766977/).
Quote verbatim when feasible: “[Exact words].” Wording influences blame inferences; direct quotes minimize reinterpretation (https://doi.org/10.3758/PBR.17.5.644).
Quantify: “[N times / for M minutes / on D dates / ~latency].” Replace vague adverbs with measurable data (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8773921/).
Remove evaluations: omit trait adjectives and “too/should” adverbs; substitute the underlying observable behavior (language framing affects judgment: https://doi.org/10.3758/PBR.17.5.644).
Remove intent clauses (e.g., “to annoy me”). Hostile intent attributions are linked with negative responding; keep to what occurred (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4243523/).

content.html: Template: “On [DATE] at [TIME] in [PLACE], I saw/heard [ACTOR] [ACTION/WORDS]. This occurred [COUNT/DURATION/LATENCY].”

items: Absolutes: flag “always/never/constantly/every time.” Prompt for timeframe and count (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6353691/).
Trait labels: flag “rude, selfish, careless, disrespectful, aggressive, lazy,” etc. Prompt: “Describe the exact behavior instead” (https://doi.org/10.3758/PBR.17.5.644).
Mind-reading: flag “on purpose,” “to hurt me,” “because you don’t care.” Prompt: “Omit intent; report the observable act” (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4243523/).
Causation claims without evidence: flag “for no reason,” “made me,” unless tied to a measurable outcome. Encourage sticking to recorded events.
Perspective-taking for later steps: I-language and checking understanding are associated with less defensive escalation (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5961625/).

items.observation: “In the past two weeks, you arrived 5–15 minutes after our agreed time on three occasions.”
items.why: Replaces global language with time-bound frequency; concreteness improves agreement (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6353691/).

items.observation: “Janice logged 62 on-site hours this week, including Saturday.”
items.why: Removes evaluative adverb; supplies measurable quantity (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8773921/).

items.evaluation: “He left the party to hurt me.”
items.observation: “He left the party without saying goodbye at 9:10 p.m.”
items.why: Strips motive attribution; hostile-attribution research cautions against inferred intent (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4243523/).

items.observation: “During the 2:00–2:15 agenda item, while I was speaking, you interrupted twice (timestamps 08:12 and 09:47).”
items.why: Replaces trait with event-bounded counts; wording shapes perceived blame (https://doi.org/10.3758/PBR.17.5.644).

sections.label: Measurement
sections.title: Measurement Concepts: Operational Definitions, ABC, Agreement

content.text: This section summarizes commonly used measurement concepts that may inform personal or professional record-keeping in observational work.

items: Operational definitions with exemplars/non-examples (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4766977/).

ABC recording with timestamps; where feasible, use continuous measures (count, duration, latency) (https://opentext.wsu.edu/ldaffin/chapter/module-5-determining-the-abcs-of-behavior-via-a-functional-assessment/; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4841258/).

Inter-observer agreement (IOA) on a sample of observations; consider statistics appropriate to the data (e.g., kappa) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10098472/; https://edpsychassociates.com/Papers/Kappa%28JEIBI%2C2004%29.pdf).
Audit for observer drift and recalibrate using reference clips/exemplars (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10098472/).

content.text: Autonomy/competence: studies and reviews describing these needs and their health associations (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5050353/; https://selfdeterminationtheory.org/topics/basic-psychological-needs/).
Belonging/social connection: advisory summarizing links to well-being and risk (https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/surgeon-general-social-connection-advisory.pdf).
Trust/safety: work connecting interpersonal trust with stress pathways (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21058850/; https://www.dignityhealth.org/articles/how-human-connection-can-relieve-stress).

items: Memory/measurement: observations depend on recall or recording fidelity; contemporaneous notes/quotes provide clearer records (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4766977/).
Intent is not adjudicated by observation: avoid hostile attributions (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4243523/).
Cultural/linguistic nuance: perceptions of “neutral” phrasing can vary; invite verification of wording.
Scope: this guide summarizes research and provides structured prompts; it does not determine clinical reliability or outcomes.
